title: What do I know?
hookLine: his motto was a question: what do I know? (Essays 2.12)

cards: Family crests. School mottoes carved over doorways. Slogans on coffee mugs.

A motto is usually a statement, sometimes a boast, often an order: be brave, be first, never surrender. Montaigne picked a motto too, in French, que sais-je, and it isn't a statement at all. It ends with a question mark.
In English: what do I know? And he gave it a picture to go with it.

teach.b: First, the question. The motto appears in his long essay called the Apology for Raymond Sebond, where he describes the ancient skeptics known as Pyrrhonists.
Their way, he says, is to doubt, to inquire, and to hold back from settling on anything. Second, why a question. Language keeps tripping them up.
Say I doubt, and you've claimed something: that you doubt. Say I know nothing, and you've claimed to know that. The idea is better held as a question, Montaigne says: what do I know?
A question claims nothing. It just keeps looking.
Third, the scales. He bears this question as a motto, he says, under the image of a balance: two pans hanging level, not tipped yet. That's the posture.
Not I'm right. Not I know nothing. Let me weigh it.
Fourth, faith and doubt. Montaigne was a Catholic, and the essay starts out as a defense of a theologian's book.
Some readers see his doubt about human reason as a way of making room for faith, of saying our minds are too small to lord it over God. Other readers see a skeptic at heart.
The essay is large enough for both readings, and this lesson doesn't pick one.
Day to day, what do I know is a small pause before a big claim: about a coworker's motives, about how a story will end, about what that text message really meant.

how: Readers of Montaigne often use que sais-je as a pause before judging: a question that keeps the scales level until the weighing is done.

s: Montaigne's motto was I know nothing
his motto was a question, what do I know?, because even I know nothing claims something.

games.q: someone you respect says something you were sure was wrong. you're Montaigne. which words do you reach for?
games.why: Montaigne says the skeptic's doubt is better held as a question. I'm right tips the scales; I know nothing is still a claim; what do I know? keeps weighing.

practice: Choose something everyday you feel sure of, not your deepest convictions, but something like what a coworker thinks of you or why a friend went quiet.
Set it on one side of the scales and ask gently: what do I know, how did I come to think this, what might I be missing? Hold the scales level, without letting them tip, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Que sais-je. French for what do I know: Montaigne's motto, a question instead of a claim, pictured as a pair of scales held level. Today's word.
